name: Ruy López Morphy Defense
summary: The Morphy Defense (3...a6) puts the question to the Spanish bishop and opens the door to the Closed, Open, and Marshall systems.
intro: The Morphy Defense arises after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6, the overwhelmingly most popular reply to the Ruy López. With a single modest pawn move Black puts the question to the b5-bishop, forcing White to declare intentions: retreat with 4.Ba4 to preserve the pin, or resolve matters with the Exchange Variation 4.Bxc6. The move ...a6 is far from a loss of time, since it gains a future tempo on the bishop with ...b5 and prepares the freeing manoeuvres that define modern Spanish theory.
line: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bb5 a6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The point of 3...a6 is to clarify the intentions of the b5-bishop before Black commits the rest of the pieces. If White retreats along the a4-e8 diagonal, Black gains the standing option of ...b5, which both hits the bishop with tempo and secures the knight tour ...Na5 to challenge it, or the fianchetto ...Bb7 to press the long diagonal. This little pawn move therefore buys space on the queenside and grants Black more control over the destiny of the light-squared bishop, the piece White would most like to trade for the c6-knight.

A crucial tactical justification underpins the whole system: White cannot simply win the e5-pawn. After 4.Bxc6 dxc6 the recapture 5.Nxe5 runs into 5...Qd4 or 5...Qg5, forking the knight and the e4-pawn and regaining the material at once. Because the pawn grab fails, White must instead build slowly with c3 and d4, castle short, and reroute the queen's knight via d2-f1-g3, while Black chooses among a rich family of set-ups. The a6-b5 structure gives Black a firm queenside foothold from which to generate counterplay against White's centre.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: White's main reply is 4.Ba4, keeping the bishop on the board and the pressure on c6. After the natural 4...Nf6 5.O-O Black reaches the great branching point of Spanish theory. The Closed lines with ...Be7, ...b5, ...d6, and ...O-O lead to the slow manoeuvring battles for which the opening is famous, while the sharp Open Variation with 5...Nxe4 grabs the pawn and invites concrete, piece-active play. The Marshall Attack, in which Black meets an early ...O-O by sacrificing a pawn with ...d5 for a lasting kingside initiative, is one of the most heavily analysed gambits in all of chess.

The principled alternative is the Exchange Variation 4.Bxc6, when 4...dxc6 hands Black the bishop pair and a semi-open d-file in return for a slightly compromised, doubled queenside pawn majority. White hopes that the resulting simplified positions and healthier kingside majority will tell in the endgame. Beyond these, the Morphy move order also embraces the Archangelsk with ...Bb7, the Steinitz Deferred with ...d6, and numerous other systems, making 3...a6 the gateway through which nearly all modern Ruy López theory flows.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The variation is named after Paul Morphy, the brilliant American who dominated mid-nineteenth-century chess and helped establish 3...a6 as the principled main line of the Spanish. Although the move had appeared earlier, Morphy's advocacy and clear understanding of its logic gave it lasting prestige, and it steadily displaced older third-move choices to become the standard answer to the Ruy López. The insight that questioning the bishop costs Black nothing concrete, while gaining useful queenside options, proved decisive for its reputation.

Over the following century the Morphy Defense became the backbone of elite opening preparation, employed by essentially every World Champion and refined through countless games and theoretical treatises. Its subsystems, from the Closed main lines to the Marshall and the Open, remain at the cutting edge of grandmaster practice, and computer analysis has only deepened their intricacies. Today 3...a6 is by a wide margin the most common continuation against the Spanish at every level of play.
